options: She don't like coffee.
She doesn't likes coffee.
She doesn't like coffee.
She isn't like coffee.
questions.tip: With he/she/it use 'doesn't' + base verb (no -s).

options: Actions happening right now
Habits and general truths
Completed past actions
Actions planned for tomorrow
questions.tip: Use Present Continuous (is/are + -ing) for actions happening right now.

options: Do he play football?
Does he plays football?
Does he play football?
Is he play football?
questions.tip: Questions with he/she/it: Does + subject + base verb (no -s).

questions.q: Which sentence uses Simple Present for a scheduled event?
options: The train leaves at 8pm.
The train is leaving at 8pm.
The train left at 8pm.
The train will be leaving at 8pm.
questions.tip: Simple Present can express timetabled future events: 'The train leaves at 8pm.'

options: He not work on Sundays.
He doesn't works on Sundays.
He doesn't work on Sundays.
He isn't work on Sundays.
questions.tip: Negative with he/she/it: doesn't + base verb (no -s on the main verb).

options: I am know the answer.
I am knowing the answer.
I know the answer.
I is knowing the answer.
questions.tip: Stative verbs (know, like, love, want) are NOT used in the continuous form.

options: General truths and permanent facts
Completed past actions
Actions happening right now or temporary situations
Habits and routines
questions.tip: Structure: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing.

options: She is work from home today.
She working from home today.
She is working from home today.
She are working from home today.
questions.tip: Subject + is/am/are + verb-ing.

questions.q: Which shows a future arrangement using Present Continuous?
options: I'm seeing the doctor tomorrow.
I see the doctor tomorrow.
I was seeing the doctor tomorrow.
I will be seeing the doctor right now.
questions.tip: Present Continuous can describe a future arrangement when a future time marker is given.

options: She is learning French.
They are working late tonight.
I am understanding the lesson.
He is reading a book.
questions.tip: 'Understand' is a stative verb — it cannot be used in the continuous form.

options: I didn't went to school.
I didn't go to school.
I don't went to school.
I wasn't go to school.
questions.tip: After 'didn't', always use the base verb (no -ed, no irregular form).

options: Actions still happening now
Completed actions at a specific time in the past
Actions that started in the past and continue
Future plans
questions.tip: Simple Past = completed action. Use time markers like 'yesterday', 'last week', 'in 2020'.

options: I have seen him yesterday.
I seen him yesterday.
I saw him yesterday.
I was see him yesterday.
questions.tip: With a specific past time (yesterday), use Simple Past, not Present Perfect.

questions.q: What is the correct past form of 'go'?
options: goed
gone
went
was go
questions.tip: 'Go' is irregular: go → went → gone.

options: She didn't went to work.
She didn't goes to work.
She didn't go to work.
She wasn't go to work.
questions.tip: Negative: didn't + base verb. No changes to the main verb.

options: They was sleeping when I called.
They were sleeping when I called.
They were sleep when I called.
They are sleeping when I called.
questions.tip: Past Continuous with 'they': were + verb-ing.

questions.q: Past Continuous is mainly used for:
options: Completed actions in the past
A background action interrupted by another (Simple Past)
Future arrangements
General past truths
questions.tip: I was cooking (background) when he arrived (interruption).

options: While I read, she was watching TV.
While I was reading, she was watching TV.
While I was read, she watched TV.
While I reading, she was watching TV.
questions.tip: Both simultaneous past actions → both in Past Continuous.

questions.q: Which sentence shows a background action interrupted by another?
options: He read when I called.
He was reading when I called.
He reading when I called.
He was read when I called.
questions.tip: Past Continuous (background) + Simple Past (interruption): was/were + -ing.

options: I was not listening to him yesterday morning.
I not was listening to him yesterday morning.
I didn't listening to him yesterday morning.
I was listen not to him yesterday morning.
questions.tip: Negative Past Continuous: was/were + not + verb-ing.

options: I have went to Paris.
I have go to Paris.
I have been to Paris.
I have being to Paris.
questions.tip: 'Have been to' = visited (and came back). 'Have gone to' = went and is still there.

questions.q: Which sentence needs Present Perfect (not Simple Past)?
options: She visited London in 2019.
She visited London last summer.
She has visited London three times.
She visited London when she was young.
questions.tip: Life experience without a specific time → Present Perfect. Specific time → Simple Past.

options: I have seen him yesterday.
I saw him yesterday.
I have saw him yesterday.
I seen him yesterday.
questions.tip: 'Yesterday' is a specific past time, so use Simple Past, not Present Perfect.

options: I live here for 10 years.
I have lived here for 10 years.
I lived here since 2015.
I have lived here since 10 years.
questions.tip: For duration still ongoing: have/has + past participle + for. Use 'since' with a start point.

options: Have you ever been to Japan?
Did you ever go to Japan?
Did you ever been to Japan?
Have you ever went to Japan?
questions.tip: Life experiences → Present Perfect. 'Have you ever + past participle?'

options: I have been study for two hours.
I have been studying for two hours.
I have studying for two hours.
I been studying for two hours.
questions.tip: Structure: have/has + been + verb-ing.

options: A completed action with a result
The duration of an ongoing activity
A past habit
A future plan
questions.tip: It stresses how long an activity has been in progress: 'I have been waiting for 2 hours.'

options: She has been work here since 2020.
She has been worked here since 2020.
She has been working here since 2020.
She is been working here since 2020.
questions.tip: have/has + been + verb-ing (not worked, not work).

options: How long has she been wait?
How long has she been waiting?
How long is she been waiting?
How long she has been waiting?
questions.tip: How long + have/has + subject + been + verb-ing?

questions.q: Which sentence uses Present Perfect Continuous INCORRECTLY?
options: I have been reading for an hour.
She has been teaching since 2010.
They have been knowing each other for years.
He has been exercising every morning.
questions.tip: 'Know' is a stative verb — use Present Perfect instead: 'have known'.

options: When I arrived, she already left.
When I arrived, she had already left.
When I arrived, she has already left.
When I arrived, she already had leave.
questions.tip: Past Perfect (had + past participle) is used for the action that happened first.

options: Two simultaneous past actions
An action completed BEFORE another past action
A current situation with past cause
A future action from a past perspective
questions.tip: 'She had left before I arrived.' — left happened first, so Past Perfect.

options: She had went home before dinner.
She had go home before dinner.
She had gone home before dinner.
She went home before dinner had started.
questions.tip: 'Go' → irregular past participle 'gone'. Structure: had + past participle.

options: By the time I arrived, the movie already started.
By the time I arrived, the movie had already started.
By the time I arrived, the movie has already started.
By the time I arrive, the movie had already started.
questions.tip: For the event that happened first in the past, use Past Perfect (had + past participle).

options: He had eaten before he left.
I had never seen snow before that day.
We didn't go because we had saw the film.
She realized she had lost her keys.
questions.tip: 'See' → irregular past participle 'seen', not 'saw'. Correct: had seen.

options: I will to call you later.
I will calling you later.
I will call you later.
I wills call you later.
questions.tip: Will + base verb (no 'to', no -ing, no -s).

options: Plans decided before speaking
Spontaneous decisions and promises
Scheduled timetable events
Past habits
questions.tip: Spontaneous: 'I'll help you!' (decided now). Pre-planned → use 'going to'.

options: I think it will rains tomorrow.
I think it will to rain tomorrow.
I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think it wills rain tomorrow.
questions.tip: After 'will', the verb stays in its base form — no changes.

questions.q: Which is correct for a prediction based on opinion?
options: I think it is going to rain.
I think it will rain.
I think it is raining.
I think it rained.
questions.tip: 'Will' is used for predictions based on opinion. 'Going to' is used with visible evidence.

options: She won't to come.
She will not come.
She will don't come.
She not will come.
questions.tip: Negative: will + not = won't or will not. Base verb follows (no 'to', no 'don't').

options: I am going study medicine.
I am going to study medicine.
I going to study medicine.
I am going to studying medicine.
questions.tip: Structure: am/is/are + going to + base verb.

questions.q: 'Going to' vs 'will' — which sentence uses the right future?
options: Look at those clouds. It will rain. (evidence visible)
Look at those clouds. It's going to rain. (evidence visible)
I'm going to answer the phone. (it just rang)
I will visit my parents next summer. (pre-planned)
questions.tip: Visible evidence → going to. Spontaneous decision → will.

options: She going to travel next month.
She is going travel next month.
She is going to travel next month.
She will going to travel next month.
questions.tip: am/is/are + going to + base verb.

options: I am not going to travel.
I am going not to travel.
I not going to travel.
I am going to not travel.
questions.tip: Negative: am/is/are + not + going to + base verb.

questions.q: Which is correct for a near-future evidence prediction?
options: Look! She will fall!
Look! She is going to fall!
Look! She falls!
Look! She would fall!
questions.tip: Visible evidence of something about to happen → going to (not will).

options: At 8pm I will be have dinner.
At 8pm I will being having dinner.
At 8pm I will be having dinner.
At 8pm I will having dinner.
questions.tip: Structure: will + be + verb-ing.

options: A completed future action
An action in progress at a specific future moment
A spontaneous decision
A past habit
questions.tip: 'This time tomorrow, I'll be flying to London.' — in progress at that future time.

options: Will you be working at 9am tomorrow?
Will you working at 9am tomorrow?
Will you be worked at 9am tomorrow?
Will you are working at 9am tomorrow?
questions.tip: Question form: Will + subject + be + verb-ing?

questions.q: Future Continuous is NOT used for:
options: Polite questions about plans
An action in progress at a future time
Completed actions
Parallel future actions
questions.tip: Completed actions use Future Perfect. Future Continuous = in progress at a future moment.

options: This time next week, I will been flying.
This time next week, I will fly.
This time next week, I will be flying.
This time next week, I am going to flying.
questions.tip: Future Continuous: will + be + verb-ing. Signals an ongoing action at a future point.

options: By Friday, I will have finish the report.
By Friday, I will have finished the report.
By Friday, I will had finished the report.
By Friday, I will finish the report.
questions.tip: Structure: will + have + past participle.

options: An action in progress at a future time
An action completed BEFORE a specific future time
A spontaneous future decision
A future habit
questions.tip: 'By 2030, they will have built the new bridge.' — completed before that future point.

questions.q: Which question uses Future Perfect correctly?
options: Will he finish the project by Monday?
Will he have finished the project by Monday?
Will he had finished the project by Monday?
Will he have finish the project by Monday?
questions.tip: Future Perfect question: Will + subject + have + past participle?

questions.q: Choose the correct Future Perfect sentence:
options: By tomorrow, she learns everything.
By tomorrow, she will be learning everything.
By tomorrow, she will have learned everything.
By tomorrow, she learned everything.
questions.tip: By + future time → Future Perfect: will + have + past participle.

questions.q: Which is NOT a signal for Future Perfect?
options: By the time
Before
Right now
By next year
questions.tip: 'Right now' signals Present Continuous — not Future Perfect.

questions.q: Which sentence is a Zero Conditional?
options: If it rains, I will stay home.
If you heat ice, it melts.
If I had money, I would travel.
If she had studied, she would have passed.
questions.tip: Zero Conditional: If + Simple Present, Simple Present. Used for scientific facts.

options: If + Past Simple, would + verb
If + Present Simple, will + verb
If + Present Simple, Present Simple
If + Past Perfect, would have + verb
questions.tip: Both clauses use Simple Present. It expresses always-true facts.

options: If you freeze water, it becomes ice.
If you freeze water, it will become ice.
If you froze water, it becomes ice.
If you freeze water, it became ice.
questions.tip: Zero Conditional: If + Present Simple, Present Simple. Both clauses are in the present.

options: Hypothetical situations
Personal predictions
Universal truths and scientific facts
Regrets about the past
questions.tip: 'If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.' — this is always true: Zero Conditional.

options: If I am tired, I will go to bed.
If I am tired, I go to bed.
If I was tired, I go to bed.
If I was tired, I went to bed.
questions.tip: Zero Conditional: Simple Present in both clauses. No will, no past tense.

options: If it will rain, I will stay home.
If it rains, I will stay home.
If it rains, I would stay home.
If it rained, I will stay home.
questions.tip: First Conditional: If + Simple Present (not will), will + base verb.

options: Imaginary or impossible situations
Real, possible future conditions
Past regrets
General truths
questions.tip: 'If it rains' is a real possibility → First Conditional.

options: If she will study, she will pass.
If she studies, she would pass.
If she studies, she will pass.
If she studied, she will pass.
questions.tip: If-clause: Simple Present. Result clause: will + base verb.

questions.q: What can replace 'if' in a First Conditional?
options: would
unless (if not)
had
were
questions.tip: 'Unless' = 'if not'. 'Unless you study, you won't pass' = 'If you don't study, you won't pass.'

options: I'll call you if I will arrive late.
I'll call you if I arrive late.
I'll call you if I arrived late.
I'll call you if I had arrived late.
questions.tip: The 'if' clause always uses Simple Present (not will/would) in First Conditional.

options: If I was you, I would apologize.
If I were you, I would apologize.
If I were you, I will apologize.
If I am you, I would apologize.
questions.tip: Second Conditional: use 'were' for ALL subjects (not 'was'), even I/he/she.

options: Real, likely future situations
Hypothetical or imaginary present/future situations
Past regrets
General facts
questions.tip: 'If I had more time' = I don't have it now. It's imaginary.

options: If I have more money, I would travel.
If I had more money, I will travel.
If I had more money, I would travel.
If I would have money, I would travel.
questions.tip: If + Past Simple, would + base verb.

questions.q: Which is a correct Second Conditional with 'unless'?
options: I would tell you unless I didn't know.
I wouldn't tell you unless I knew.
I would tell you unless I know.
I would tell you unless I will know.
questions.tip: Second Conditional: would + base verb in main clause, Past Simple in if/unless clause.

questions.q: Choose the correct modal alternative to 'would' in Second Conditional:
options: If I had time, I might help you.
If I had time, I must help you.
If I had time, I will help you.
If I had time, I should to help you.
questions.tip: In Second Conditional, 'might' or 'could' can replace 'would' to soften the certainty.

options: If I had studied, I would pass.
If I had studied, I would have passed.
If I would have studied, I would have passed.
If I studied, I would have passed.
questions.tip: Third Conditional: If + Past Perfect, would have + past participle.

options: A real future possibility
A present imaginary situation
A past situation that didn't happen (regret)
A general truth
questions.tip: 'If I had known' means I didn't know → it's a past regret.

options: She would have went if she had known.
She would have go if she had known.
She would have gone if she had known.
She would gone if she had known.
questions.tip: would have + past participle. 'Go' → 'gone'.

options: If he had been more careful, the accident could have been avoided.
If he has been more careful, the accident could have been avoided.
If he was more careful, the accident could be avoided.
If he had been more careful, the accident can have been avoided.
questions.tip: Third Conditional: If + Past Perfect, could/would/might + have + past participle.

questions.q: What is the meaning of: 'If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the train'?
options: I left early and caught the train.
I didn't leave early, so I missed the train.
I will leave early to catch the train.
I always miss the train when I leave early.
questions.tip: Third Conditional refers to a past situation that didn't happen — the opposite is true.

questions.q: Which sentence is a Mixed Conditional (past condition → present result)?
options: If I studied, I would pass.
If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If I had studied, I would have passed.
If I study, I will pass.
questions.tip: Mixed: If + Past Perfect (past condition), would + base verb (present result).

options: Both clauses refer to the same time
The condition and the result refer to different times
Both clauses are in the present
The condition is future and the result is past
questions.tip: Past condition + present result, or present state + past result.

questions.q: Which Mixed Conditional is correct (present state → past result)?
options: If I were braver, I would have spoken up.
If I had been braver, I would speak up.
If I was braver, I would spoken up.
If I am braver, I would have spoken up.
questions.tip: Present state → past result: If + Past Simple (were), would + have + past participle.

questions.q: Which Mixed Conditional is correct (past cause → present result)?
options: If I had taken the job, I would be rich now.
If I took the job, I would have been rich now.
If I had taken the job, I would have been rich.
If I would take the job, I would be rich now.
questions.tip: Past cause → present result: If + Past Perfect, would + base verb.

questions.q: When do we use a Mixed Conditional?
options: When both clauses are about the same time
When condition and result are in different time frames
When making polite requests
When expressing general truths
questions.tip: Mixed Conditionals combine different time frames — usually past condition + present result, or vice versa.

questions.q: Which is the correct passive form of 'They built this house in 1900'?
options: This house was build in 1900.
This house built in 1900.
This house was built in 1900.
This house has built in 1900.
questions.tip: Passive: was/were + past participle. 'Build' → irregular past participle 'built'.

options: The subject is the most important element
The agent (doer) is unknown, obvious, or unimportant
You want to emphasize who did the action
The action happened in the future
questions.tip: 'The car was stolen.' — we don't know (or care) who stole it.

options: The report will be finish by Friday.
The report will be finished by Friday.
The report will been finished by Friday.
The report will have finished by Friday.
questions.tip: Future Passive: will + be + past participle.

options: The letter has been sent.
The letter have been sent.
The letter has been send.
The letter was been sent.
questions.tip: Present Perfect Passive: has/have + been + past participle.

questions.q: Which active sentence converts correctly to passive?
options: Active: 'He writes the report.' → Passive: 'The report is writing by him.'
Active: 'He writes the report.' → Passive: 'The report is written by him.'
Active: 'He writes the report.' → Passive: 'The report was written by him.'
Active: 'He writes the report.' → Passive: 'The report is being written by him.'
questions.tip: Simple Present Passive: is/are + past participle. 'write' → 'written'.

questions.q: Direct: 'I love pizza.' → Reported: She said...
options: ...that she loves pizza.
...that she loved pizza.
...that she will love pizza.
...that she is loving pizza.
questions.tip: In reported speech, Simple Present → Simple Past (backshift).

questions.q: Direct: 'I will call you.' → Reported: He said...
options: ...that he will call me.
...that he calls me.
...that he would call me.
...that he had called me.
questions.tip: In reported speech, 'will' → 'would'.

options: She said me she was tired.
She told me she was tired.
She told to me she was tired.
She said to me that she were tired.
questions.tip: 'Say' doesn't take an object directly. 'Tell' requires a person: tell me, tell her.

questions.q: Direct: 'I am tired.' → Reported: She said...
options: ...that she is tired.
...that she was tired.
...that she will be tired.
...that she had been tired.
questions.tip: Backshift: Simple Present → Simple Past. 'is' → 'was'.

questions.q: Direct: 'Don't touch that!' → Reported: He told me...
options: ...not touch that.
...to not touch that.
...don't touch that.
...not to touch that.
questions.tip: Reported commands (negative): tell + object + not to + base verb.

options: She cans speak French.
She can speaks French.
She can to speak French.
She can speak French.
questions.tip: Modals (can, will, must, should) + base verb. No 's', no 'to', no -ing.

questions.q: 'Must' vs 'Have to' — which expresses external obligation (a rule imposed by someone else)?
options: You must be home by midnight. (parent's rule)
You have to wear a uniform. (school rule)
You must try this cake! (strong recommendation)
You must be joking. (deduction)
questions.tip: 'Have to' = external rule. 'Must' = speaker's own obligation or deduction.

options: You must see a doctor. (obligation)
You should see a doctor. (advice)
You can see a doctor. (ability/permission)
You will see a doctor. (prediction)
questions.tip: 'Should' = advice or recommendation. 'Must' = strong obligation.

options: I must to go now.
I should to leave.
I might be late.
She would to help.
questions.tip: Modals are followed by the base verb without 'to'.

options: She must be at home. (deduction — very likely)
She might be at home. (possibility)
She can't be at home. (near certainty — impossible)
She has to be at home. (external obligation)
questions.tip: 'Might' = possibility (maybe). 'Must' = strong deduction (almost certain).

options: She is engineer.
She is a engineer.
She is an engineer.
She is the engineer.
questions.tip: 'Engineer' starts with a vowel sound (/ɛ/) → use 'an'.

options: The life is short.
The dogs are friendly. (general statement)
I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.
I play the tennis.
questions.tip: Use 'the' on second mention — both speaker and listener know which dog.

options: I love the music. (general)
Music is beautiful. (general)
The music is beautiful. (general)
A music is beautiful.
questions.tip: General statements about uncountable nouns → no article. 'Music is beautiful.'

options: She plays piano very well.
She plays a piano very well.
She plays the piano very well.
She plays the piano very good.
questions.tip: Musical instruments always take 'the': play the piano, the guitar, the violin.

options: He is a honest man.
He is an honest man.
He is the honest man.
He is honest man.
questions.tip: 'Honest' begins with a silent H, so the vowel sound /ɒ/ follows → use 'an', not 'a'.

options: I was born in April 12th.
I was born on April 12th.
I was born at April 12th.
I was born by April 12th.
questions.tip: Specific dates → 'on'. Months → 'in'. Times → 'at'.

options: She started working on 2019.
She started working at 2019.
She started working in 2019.
She started working by 2019.
questions.tip: Years → 'in'. Days → 'on'. Clock times → 'at'.

options: I'll see you on the morning.
I'll see you in the morning.
I'll see you at the morning.
I'll see you by the morning.
questions.tip: Parts of the day: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. Exception: at night.

options: The meeting is in Monday.
The meeting is on Monday.
The meeting is at Monday.
The meeting is by Monday.
questions.tip: Days of the week → 'on': on Monday, on Tuesday, on Christmas Day.

options: I'll finish it at the end of the week.
I'll finish it in the end of the week.
I'll finish it on the end of the week.
I'll finish it by the end of the week.
questions.tip: 'By' expresses a deadline — 'by the end of the week' = no later than that point.

options: The keys are in the table.
The keys are at the table.
The keys are on the table.
The keys are by the table.
questions.tip: 'On' = surface. 'In' = enclosed space. 'At' = specific point/location.

options: She lives in Paris.
She lives on Paris.
She lives at Paris.
She lives by Paris.
questions.tip: Cities and countries → 'in'. Specific points → 'at'.

options: There's a fly on my soup.
There's a fly in my soup.
There's a fly at my soup.
There's a fly by my soup.
questions.tip: 'In' = inside a container or enclosed space.

options: I live in the second floor.
I live on the second floor.
I live at the second floor.
I live by the second floor.
questions.tip: Floors in a building: 'on the first/second floor' (not 'in' or 'at').

options: She hid the letter at the book.
She hid the letter by the book.
She hid the letter in the book.
She hid the letter on the book.
questions.tip: 'In' = inside/enclosed space. A letter placed inside a book: 'in the book'.

options: I enjoy to swim.
I enjoy swimming.
I enjoy swim.
I enjoy to swimming.
questions.tip: 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund (-ing), never by an infinitive.

options: She wants going to Paris.
She wants go to Paris.
She wants to go to Paris.
She wants to going to Paris.
questions.tip: 'Want' is always followed by an infinitive (to + base verb).

questions.q: 'Stop smoking' vs 'Stop to smoke' — what's the difference?
options: They mean the same thing.
'Stop smoking' = quit the habit. 'Stop to smoke' = pause in order to smoke.
'Stop to smoke' = quit the habit. 'Stop smoking' = pause to smoke.
Neither is correct.
questions.tip: Gerund after 'stop' = quit. Infinitive after 'stop' = purpose (stop in order to).

options: He's good at to cook.
He's good at cook.
He's good at cooking.
He's good to cook.
questions.tip: After prepositions (at, in, about, for...), always use the gerund (-ing).

options: Don't forget calling your mom. (a future task)
Don't forget to call your mom. (a future task)
Don't forget to calling your mom.
Don't forget call your mom.
questions.tip: 'Forget to do' = forget a future task. 'Forget doing' = forget a past experience.

options: The man which called me was my boss.
The man who called me was my boss.
The man that called me was my boss.
B and C are both correct.
questions.tip: For people, use 'who' or 'that' in defining relative clauses.

questions.q: Which sentence has a non-defining relative clause?
options: The book that I bought is great.
My sister, who lives in London, is a doctor.
The city where I grew up is small.
The man who called was my boss.
questions.tip: Non-defining = extra info between commas. Defining = essential info, no commas.

questions.q: Which is correct in a non-defining clause?
options: My brother, that is a doctor, lives in NY.
My brother, who is a doctor, lives in NY.
My brother who is a doctor lives in NY.
My brother, which is a doctor, lives in NY.
questions.tip: 'That' cannot be used in non-defining relative clauses. Use 'who' for people.

options: The city which I was born is beautiful.
The city where I was born is beautiful.
The city that I was born is beautiful.
The city who I was born is beautiful.
questions.tip: 'Where' replaces a place in relative clauses.

questions.q: Which sentence can omit the relative pronoun?
options: The man who is standing there is my uncle. (subject)
The woman who I spoke to is my teacher. (object)
The house which was built in 1800 is famous. (subject)
The man whose car was stolen called the police. (possessive)
questions.tip: Object relative pronouns (who, which, that) can be omitted: 'The woman I spoke to is my teacher.'

options: She is more taller than her brother.
She is tallest than her brother.
She is taller than her brother.
She is the taller than her brother.
questions.tip: Short adjectives: add -er + than (not 'more'). Never both together.

options: This is the most tallest building.
This is the tallest building.
This is the more tall building.
This is tallest building.
questions.tip: Superlative of short adjectives: the + -est. Never 'most' with -est.

options: gooder
more good
better
best
questions.tip: Irregular: good → better → best.

options: She is the most intelligent student in the class.
She is the more intelligent student in the class.
She is most intelligent student in the class.
She is more intelligent student in the class.
questions.tip: Long adjectives (3+ syllables): the most + adjective. Always use 'the' with superlatives.

questions.q: What is the correct comparative of 'bad'?
options: badder
more bad
worst
worse
questions.tip: Irregular: bad → worse → worst.

options: Where she lives?
Where does she lives?
Where does she live?
Where is she live?
questions.tip: Wh- questions: Wh-word + auxiliary (does) + subject + base verb.

questions.q: Which is the correct subject question?
options: Who did call you?
Who called you?
Who does call you?
Who is called you?
questions.tip: When 'who' is the subject, NO auxiliary needed: Who called? (not 'Who did call?')

options: You like coffee, don't you?
You like coffee, do you?
You like coffee, aren't you?
You like coffee, isn't it?
questions.tip: Positive statement + negative tag. 'Like' → auxiliary 'do' → tag: don't you?

options: Can you tell me where does she live?
Can you tell me where she lives?
Can you tell me where she does live?
Can you tell me where is she living?
questions.tip: Indirect questions use normal word order (not inverted): 'where she lives' (not 'where does she live').

options: Do you prefer coffee, do you?
You prefer coffee or tea?
Would you prefer coffee or tea?
Are you prefer coffee or tea?
questions.tip: Choice questions for offers/preferences: Would you prefer A or B?

options: She gave me an advice.
She gave me some advices.
She gave me some advice.
She gave me an advices.
questions.tip: 'Advice' is uncountable — no plural, no 'a/an'. Use 'some advice' or 'a piece of advice'.

options: How many water do you drink?
How much water do you drink?
How many waters do you drink?
How much waters do you drink?
questions.tip: 'Water' is uncountable → 'how much'. Countable nouns → 'how many'.

options: I have many informations.
I need some furnitures.
There is a news on TV.
I have a little free time.
questions.tip: 'A little' is correct with uncountable nouns. Information, furniture, and news are all uncountable.

options: Can I have a bread?
Can I have some bread?
Can I have some breads?
Can I have an bread?
questions.tip: 'Bread' is uncountable — use 'some bread' or 'a slice/loaf of bread' (never 'a bread').

questions.q: Which pair is correct (countable vs uncountable)?
options: Work (countable) / job (uncountable)
Work (uncountable) / job (countable)
Work (uncountable) / job (uncountable)
Work (countable) / job (countable)
questions.tip: 'Work' is usually uncountable ('a lot of work'). 'Job' is countable ('two jobs').

options: Give something to someone above you
Quit or stop doing something
Return something
Start doing something new
questions.tip: 'Give up' is idiomatic — it means quit/stop, not literally give something up.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct (separable phrasal verb)?
options: Turn off it.
Turn it off.
Turn the television off it.
It off turn.
questions.tip: With pronouns, the object must go BETWEEN verb and particle: turn it off (not 'turn off it').

options: She looked after her grandmother.
She looked her grandmother after.
She looked after her grandmother it.
She looked her after grandmother.
questions.tip: Inseparable phrasal verbs (look after, look for, get on) keep verb and particle together.

options: To start running
To have no more of something
To escape from somewhere
To exceed a limit
questions.tip: 'Run out of' = have no more left: 'We ran out of milk' = there's no milk left.

options: I came across an old photo.
I came an old photo across.
I came across to an old photo.
I across came an old photo.
questions.tip: 'Come across' = find by chance. It is inseparable: you cannot split verb and particle.

options: Everyone are ready.
Everyone is ready.
Everyone were ready.
Everyone be ready.
questions.tip: Indefinite pronouns (everyone, someone, nobody, each) always take a singular verb.

options: The news are shocking.
The news were shocking.
The news is shocking.
The news be shocking.
questions.tip: 'News' looks plural but is uncountable and singular: 'the news is'.

options: Mathematics are difficult.
Mathematics is difficult.
Mathematics were difficult.
Mathematics have been difficult.
questions.tip: Subjects ending in -ics (mathematics, physics, economics) take a singular verb.

options: Neither of them are ready.
Neither of them is ready.
Neither of they is ready.
Neither of them was being ready.
questions.tip: 'Neither of + plural noun' takes a singular verb in formal English.

options: A number of students was absent.
A number of students were absent.
The number of students were absent.
A number of students are was absent.
questions.tip: 'A number of' = many → plural verb. 'The number of' = the total count → singular verb.

options: I use to smoke.
I used to smoke.
I am used to smoke.
I was used to smoking.
questions.tip: 'Used to' + base verb = past habit that no longer exists.

questions.q: 'I am used to waking up early' means:
options: I woke up early in the past but not anymore
I am accustomed to waking up early (it's normal for me)
I need to start waking up early
I will wake up early
questions.tip: 'Be used to' + gerund = accustomed to. 'Used to' + base verb = past habit.

options: I am used to wake up early.
I am used to waking up early.
I used to waking up early.
I am used to woke up early.
questions.tip: 'Be used to' is always followed by a gerund (-ing) or noun.

questions.q: Which is the correct question form of 'used to'?
options: Did you used to play chess?
Used you to play chess?
Did you use to play chess?
Do you used to play chess?
questions.tip: In questions/negatives, 'used to' loses the -d: 'Did you use to...?' (not 'did you used to').

options: She got used to drive on the left.
She got used to driving on the left.
She is used to drive on the left.
She got used to drove on the left.
questions.tip: 'Get/be used to' is followed by a gerund (-ing) or noun, never an infinitive.

options: I wish I have more time.
I wish I had more time.
I wish I would have more time.
I wish I will have more time.
questions.tip: Wish for present situations: wish + Past Simple (not present, not would).

questions.q: To express a past regret with 'wish':
options: I wish I didn't say that.
I wish I haven't said that.
I wish I hadn't said that.
I wish I didn't said that.
questions.tip: Wish + Past Perfect = regret about the past.

questions.q: 'I wish you would stop talking' expresses:
options: A past regret
A desire for someone to change their current behavior
An impossible present situation
A future plan
questions.tip: Wish + would = annoyance or desire for change in someone else's behavior.

options: If only I will be taller.
If only I am taller.
If only I were taller.
If only I had be taller.
questions.tip: 'If only' works like 'wish': use Past Simple (were) for present situations.

options: will stop
stopped
would stop
has stopped
questions.tip: Wish + would = annoyance, wanting a change: 'I wish it would stop raining.'
